lead: The nozzle is the last part of the fuel system that touches the fuel. It turns high pressure into a spray of tiny droplets, gives the spray a direction and a shape, and sets how far the spray reaches into the cylinder before it mixes with air. Hole size, hole number, opening pressure and injection pressure decide atomisation, penetration and cone angle. Every diesel engine's smoke, starting and fuel economy depends on getting this small part right.
prereq: You need: rail and injection pressure from chapter 2.4, and injector construction from chapter 2.5.

sections.h3: The injector, nozzle types, opening pressure and sac volume

blocks.text: The fuel injector (nozzle holder) is the body that carries the nozzle into the cylinder head. Fuel from the high-pressure pipe runs down a drilling to the nozzle. A spindle and spring press the needle onto its seat, and an adjusting screw or shims set the spring force. Fuel that leaks past the needle to lubricate it returns through a leak-off pipe.

The nozzle is a hardened needle on a conical seat with one or more holes below it. When fuel pressure on the needle's lifting area beats the spring, the needle lifts and fuel escapes. That pressure is the opening pressure; diesel nozzles commonly open between about 100 and 250 bar, direct injection at the higher end.

items: Pintle nozzle: a pin (pintle) through a single hole leaves an annular gap and gives a hollow-cone spray with short penetration; used in indirect-injection chambers.
Single-hole nozzle: one plain hole; simple and cheap, for some indirect-injection chambers.
Multi-hole (multi-orifice) nozzle: 3 to 10 holes of about 0.1 to 0.4 mm, the smallest on modern common-rail nozzles, each aimed at a part of the bowl; the standard for direct injection.
Throttle (delay) nozzle: a pintle shaped so the flow area stays small at low needle lift; less fuel enters during the delay period, so the pressure rise is softer.

blocks.text: Below the seat is a small cavity, the sac. Fuel trapped there when the needle closes dribbles out late and burns badly, adding unburnt hydrocarbons and smoke. A valve-covered-orifice (VCO) nozzle lets the needle cover the holes and removes the sac.

sections.h3: Nozzle tests: pop test, spray and leak

blocks.text: A nozzle is tested on a pop tester: a hand pump, a pressure gauge and a holder.

items: Fill the tester with clean diesel and clamp the injector in the holder, spray pointing into a collector.
Pump slowly and watch the gauge. The pressure at which the needle lifts is the opening pressure; compare it with the maker's value and correct it with the screw or shims.
Watch the spray: a fine, even mist from every hole, the same on each; a solid stream, a drip or a blocked hole means a worn or dirty nozzle.
Leak test: hold the pressure about 10 to 20 bar below the opening pressure; the gauge should stay nearly steady and the tip dry for the stated time.

blocks.text: A sharp chatter during the pop shows the needle is free and seating. Keep hands away: fuel at these pressures can pierce skin.

sections.h3: Spray formation, droplet size, cone angle and penetration

blocks.text: A jet leaving a small hole is unstable: air drag and turbulence tear it into ligaments, then drops. Droplet size is given as the Sauter mean diameter (SMD, D₃₂), the diameter of a drop with the same volume-to-surface ratio as the whole spray; diesel sprays are often 10 to 30 μm.

blocks.where: ṁ is the fuel mass flow (kg/s); C<sub>d</sub> is the discharge coefficient (about 0.7); A is the total hole area (m²); ρ is the fuel density (about 830 kg/m³); Δp is injection minus cylinder pressure (Pa).

blocks.text: Penetration S is the distance the spray tip has reached from the nozzle at time t after the start of injection. A widely used fit (Hiroyasu and Arai) has the tip moving at constant speed until the jet breaks up at tb, and then:

S = 2.95 (Δp ÷ ρa)0.25 √(d t)
S in m; ρa is the cylinder air density (kg/m³); d is the hole diameter (m); t in s. Penetration grows as the fourth root of pressure but as the square root of hole size, and falls in denser air.

items: Cone angle: the angle of one jet, often 10° to 25°; the angle between opposite jets of a multi-hole nozzle is much larger.
Penetration must match the bowl: too short leaves outer air unused, too long wets the wall and makes smoke and oil dilution.
Higher injection pressure: finer drops, faster mixing, a little longer penetration.
More, smaller holes at the same total area: better atomisation but weaker jets that penetrate less.
Denser air (turbocharging): more drag, shorter penetration, wider cone.

examples.question: A nozzle has 5 holes of 0.25 mm diameter and C<sub>d</sub> = 0.7. Injection pressure is 700 bar and cylinder pressure 60 bar; diesel density 830 kg/m³, air density in the cylinder 20 kg/m³. Find the total hole area, the fuel flow, the fuel per injection for 1.0 ms and the spray penetration 0.5 ms after the start.
steps: Break-up time t<sub>b</sub> = 28.65 ρ d ÷ √(ρ<sub>a</sub>Δp) = 28.65 × 830 × 0.25×10⁻³ ÷ √(20 × 6.4×10⁷) = 0.166 ms, so at 0.5 ms the second formula applies.
examples.answer: A = 0.245 mm², ṁ = 0.056 kg/s, 56 mg in 1 ms, and the tip is about 44 mm out at 0.5 ms; in a bowl of 35 mm radius the jets would reach the wall, so the designer would use smaller holes or more swirl.

traps: Putting the diameter straight into A = π d² and forgetting the divide by 4. A 0.25 mm hole gives 4.909×10⁻⁸ m², not 1.96×10⁻⁷ m².

Mixing opening pressure with injection pressure. Opening pressure is set by the nozzle spring (the needle lift point, around 100–250 bar). Injection pressure is the pump or rail pressure, which is much higher.

Saying more holes always means a better spray. More holes at the same total area make each hole smaller: atomisation improves, but each jet is weaker, penetrates less, and jets may merge in a small chamber.
Confusing pintle and throttle nozzles. Both have a pin in the hole; only the throttle nozzle's pin is shaped to throttle the flow at low needle lift.
Forgetting sac volume. The fuel trapped below the needle seat after closing burns late and adds hydrocarbons and smoke, so a worn sac is a real fault, not a detail.

quiz.a: The fuel pressure at which the needle lifts off its seat against the spring and fuel starts to spray. It is fixed by the spring setting.

quiz.q: Name the four nozzle types and one use of each.
quiz.a: Pintle (hollow cone, older small DI and IDI engines), single-hole (small engines, some IDI), multi-hole or multi-orifice (3–8 holes, direct-injection diesel), throttle (pintle shaped to cut early flow, reduces diesel knock).

quiz.q: Why does a throttle nozzle reduce diesel knock?
quiz.a: It keeps the flow area small at low needle lift, so the early fuel delivery is slow. Less fuel collects in the chamber during the ignition delay, so the premixed burn and the pressure rise are gentler.

quiz.q: Why is a small sac volume wanted?
quiz.a: Fuel trapped in the sac cannot be timed and escapes late as the pressure falls. It evaporates after the main burn and burns poorly, adding unburnt hydrocarbons and smoke. VCO nozzles remove the sac.

quiz.q: Injection pressure difference is doubled and the hole diameter is halved. Using S ∝ Δp<sup>0.25</sup> √d, find the change in penetration at the same time, and in flow per hole.
quiz.a: Penetration ratio = 2<sup>0.25</sup> × √0.5 = 1.189 × 0.707 = 0.84, about 16 % shorter. Flow per hole ∝ d²√Δp = 0.25 × 1.414 = 0.35 of before, so more holes or a longer injection are needed; atomisation improves.

quiz.q: A turbocharged diesel has good atomisation but smokes at full load, and inspection shows dry black deposits on the piston crown near the wall. Give the likely cause and two changes.
quiz.a: The spray is penetrating too far and wetting the wall, so the fuel there burns rich and leaves soot. Reduce penetration with more, smaller holes, lower injection pressure at full load, or more swirl to bend the jets; also check for a worn nozzle with a large sac.

quiz.q: A pop tester shows an opening pressure 15 bar below the maker's value, and the needle drips at low pressure. State the fault and the remedy.
quiz.a: The spring has weakened or the needle and seat are worn, so the needle lifts too early and does not seal. Re-shim or replace the nozzle and set the opening pressure with shims on the spring, then repeat the pop test and leak test.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production common-rail nozzles use 7 to 10 holes of about 0.1 mm, cut by EDM or laser and shaped to control the cone. Spray research uses X-ray imaging and optical engines to measure droplets inside a running cylinder (see combustion visualization). Search next for Sauter mean diameter correlations, spray penetration correlations and VCO versus sac nozzles.
